title: Where components can run: subnets, zones and regions

tiers.edge: Public subnets (route to the internet gateway)

ext.why: An external system runs outside your network. Reach it through private connectivity, a VPN or the egress gateway.

saas.why: A SaaS service runs in the vendor's network, not in your subnets. Reach it through a private link or the egress gateway.

dns.why: DNS traffic steering is a global service: it answers from the provider's edge, not from a subnet or a region.

cdn.why: A CDN is global: it runs at the provider's edge locations, not in your subnets.

waf.why: The WAF is attached to the CDN, load balancer or API gateway it protects; it has no place in a subnet.

queue.why: A managed queue is a regional service outside your VPC: the provider runs it across all zones. Reach it privately through an interface endpoint in your subnet.

obj.why: Object storage is a regional service outside your VPC, stored across zones by the provider. Reach it privately through a gateway or interface endpoint.

kms.why: Key management is a regional service outside your VPC. Reach it through an interface endpoint.

sec.why: The secrets manager is a regional service outside your VPC. Reach it through an interface endpoint.

mon.why: Observability is a regional service outside your VPC. Ship telemetry through an interface endpoint.

reg.why: The container registry is a regional service outside your VPC. Pull images through an interface endpoint.

art.why: The artifact store is a regional service outside your VPC.

llm.why: Foundation-model APIs are regional services outside your VPC. Call them privately through an interface endpoint (for example PrivateLink for Bedrock).

idp.why: A managed identity provider is a regional service outside your VPC.

gw.why: A managed API gateway is a regional service outside your VPC. A private API is reached through an interface endpoint; its back ends can be in your subnets.

pros: Internet-facing load balancers need public subnets in at least two zones
Keeps the application subnets private
Reachable from the internet
cons: Shares the edge subnets with other public endpoints: a wider blast radius

pros: An internal load balancer between services
cons: Not reachable from the internet

if_internet_facing.why: It receives internet traffic, and an internet-facing load balancer must be in public subnets with a route to the internet gateway. Private subnets have none.

data.why: Isolated data subnets have no internet route and are meant only for data stores. Put the load balancer in the ingress or application subnets.

pros: Internal only
cons: Mixes application traffic into the shared-services subnets

pros: A NAT gateway lives in a public subnet so it can reach the internet gateway
Public subnet with an internet route
cons: Shares the ingress subnets

app.why: A NAT or egress gateway must sit in a public subnet with a route to the internet gateway; the private subnets send their traffic to it.

data.why: Isolated subnets have no internet route, so an egress gateway cannot work there.

platform.why: The shared-services subnets are private: an egress gateway needs a public subnet.

pros: Private: no public addresses
Outbound only through NAT and the egress firewall
No NAT cost for outbound calls
cons: Instances get public addresses: exposed to scanning and attack
Breaks the layered network (EA-P5)

cons: Instances exposed to the internet

notify.why: A managed notification service or event bus is regional and runs outside your VPC. Publish to it through an interface endpoint.

pros: Lower latency and no cross-zone data charges between components in the same zone
cons: A zone outage takes every instance down
Fails a multi-zone resilience target

lb.why: An Application Load Balancer needs subnets in at least two zones; it cannot be pinned to one zone.

pros: Fewer network interfaces to manage
cons: Functions attached to one subnet stop when that zone fails; give them a subnet in each zone

pros: Chooses where the primary runs, next to the application
cons: The standby still runs in another zone; only the primary moves

pros: A NAT gateway is zonal: one per zone is the resilient pattern
cons: Instances in other zones that use it pay cross-zone charges and lose egress if this zone fails
